newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries trim losses after Beige Book report.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries trim losses after Beige Book report.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices trimmed losses at midday on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve released its Beige Book, an anecdotal description of business and economic conditions across the nation.
"The market picked up a couple of ticks on the Beige Book," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Lieberman said the market expected the Fed to say that inflation pressures were building and he said the Fed Beige Book did say that, "but not quite so directly."

The market paid the most attention to the Fed's view of the nation's labor force, analysts said. That view was consistent with remarks Fed officials, including Fed Governor Janet Yellen, have recently made in published interviews.

"The sum of it is that the Fed sees the labor market as tight," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "They see some wage pressures building. They don't see those pressures translating into price pressures yet, but clearly the concern is that is going to happen eventually."
Feinman said the Beige Book report did nothing to change the view that "the Fed is on course to raise interest rates by 25 basis points" at its September 24 policy meeting.
Lieberman said the Fed's characterization of inflation signs as inconclusive does not mean the central bank won't raise rates.

"The signs won't be conclusive until inflation actually rises and by then it will be too late," he said. "The trajectory here is pretty straightforward. The Beige Book doesn't say that prices are rising but then neither do the monthly price indices."
The Fed said that while the manufacturing sector is expanding or holding at a high level, it was encountering few capacity constraints.
But Lieberman noted that the Fed's inflation concerns currently lie not with the manufacturing sector, but with the labor market.
At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were up two basis points to 5.17 percent and six-month bill rates were down three basis points to 5.30 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-19/32, yielding 6.35 percent.
Five-year notes were down 2/32 to 99-4/32, yielding 6.71 percent.
Ten-year notes slipped 4/32 to 100-12/32, yielding 6.94 percent.
